ἐκπέμψαι καὶ ἰδεῖν, εἰ καὶ ἀληθῆ τὰ λεγόμενα. Ἐν τούτοις οὖν ὁ χρόνος ἐτρίβετο.
Πρὸς δὴ τούτοις, ὅτε τὸ ἀληθὲς ἔγνωσαν, βασιλεῖς ὄντες καὶ ἐκδημεῖν μέλλοντες,
ἀνάγκην εἶχον πρότερον εὖ διαθεῖναι τὰ κατὰ τὸν οἶκον, καὶ ἐπιστῆσαι τοῖς
ἀρχομένοις τοὺς ἀνθ' ἑαυτῶν. Ταῦτα πάντα αὐτοὺς ἀπησχόλει, καὶ ἐνε βράδυνον.
Καὶ εἰ μὴ σφόδρα γε ἀγαπητοί τινες ἦσαν καὶ δίκαιοι, οὐκ ἂν, τὰς οἰκείας
καταλιπόντες χώρας καὶ βασιλείας, ἀφικνοῦντο πρὸς τὴν ἐπίσκεψιν, ἀλλὰ δι'
ἑτέρων τὴν χρείαν ἐπλήρουν. Ἔστι δὲ ἐννοεῖν, ὡς καὶ οἰκονομία τις ἦν θεία τῆς
ἀφίξεως ἡ ἀναβολή. Ἐπειδὴ γὰρ ὁμοῦ τῇ τῶν φίλων διαλέξει καὶ τὸ πᾶν τοῦ ἀγῶνος
ἐλύθη, τοῦ Θεοῦ χρηματίσαντος, καὶ τὸν δίκαιον ἀνακτησαμένου καὶ
στεφανώσαντος, οἰκονο μία τις γέγονε θεία, ἐμβραδῦναι τοὺς φίλους, ἵνα παραταθῇ
τὰ τοῦ νοσήματος, καὶ μειζόνως ἀθλή σας ὁ δίκαιος, δικαιότερον ἀναῤῥηθῇ παρὰ τοῦ
Θεοῦ. Στίχ. ιαʹ. Καὶ παρεγένοντο πρὸς αὐτὸν ὁμοθυ μαδὸν, τοῦ παρακαλέσαι καὶ
ἐπισκέψασθαι αὐτόν. Ὁ Σύμμαχος οὕτως ἐξέδωκε· Συνετάξαντο γὰρ ὁμοῦ ἐλθόντες
συμπαθῆσαι αὐτῷ, καὶ παραμυ θήσασθαι αὐτόν. Ὅρα καὶ ἐντεῦθεν, ὡς καὶ ἕτερος
παρῆλθε χρόνος, ἕως ὅτε, πρὸς ἀλλήλους διαπεμψά μενοι, τὴν ἐπὶ τὸ αὐτὸ σύνοδόν
τε καὶ ἄφιξιν ἐποιή σαντο. Στίχ. ιβʹ. Καὶ καταπασάμενοι γῆν ἐπὶ τὰς κεφαλὰς αὐτῶν.
Στίχ. ιγʹ. Παρεκάθισαν αὐτῷ ἑπτὰ ἡμέρας, καὶ ἑπτὰ νύκτας. Οὐκ εἶπε δὲ ἡ Γραφὴ, ὅτι
παρεκάθηντο ἑπτὰ ἡμέρας πρωΐθεν ἕως ἑσπέρας, οὐδὲ ἑπτὰ νύκτας ἀφ' ἑσπέρας
μέχρι πρωΐ. ∆ῆλον οὖν, ὅτι, τὸ πλεῖον τῆς ἡμέρας παρακαθεζόμενοι, ὑπεχώρουν τὰς
ἀναγκαίας ἐκπληρώσοντες χρείας· καὶ πάλιν ἐπανήκοντες, μέ χρι πολλοῦ τῆς νυκτὸς
παρεκαθέζοντο, καὶ αὖθις ἀπιόντες, πάλιν ὤρθριζον πρὸς αὐτόν. Ὃ δὴ τῶν
γνησιωτάτων καὶ συμπαθεστάτων φίλων ἴδιον. Τῇ δὲ κοινῇ συνηθείᾳ χρωμένη ἡ
Γραφὴ, οὕτως ἀπολύτως εἶπε· Παρεκάθισαν αὐτῷ ἑπτὰ ἡμέρας καὶ ἑπτὰ νύκτας. Ἐπεὶ
καὶ ὅτε λέγει τὸν Ἰακὼβ δεκατέσσαρα ἔτη δουλεῦσαι, καὶ συγκαίεσθαι τῷ καύσονι
τῆς ἡμέρας καὶ τῷ παγετῷ τῆς νυκτὸς, ἆρα ὑπὸ στέ γην οὐκ εἰσῄει ποτέ; ἆρα
οὐδεμιᾶς ἀναπαύσεως ἔτυχεν ὅλῳ τῷ χρόνῳ; Ταῦτα μὲν οὖν καὶ λεπτολο γεῖν
φλύαρον. Ὡς γὰρ ἔφην, ἡ Γραφὴ κοινῇ συνη θείᾳ χρῆται. Ἐπειδὴ δέ τινες,
κωμῳδοῦντες τὴν Γραφὴν, καὶ ἐντεῦθεν αὐτὴν ὡς ψευδῆ διασύρουσιν· Ὡς γὰρ ἂν,
φασὶν, ἄσιτοι διετέλουν καὶ ἄϋπνοι ἐπὶ τοσαύταις ἡμέραις; ἠναγκάσθημεν αὐτῶν
συνα παχθῆναι τῇ ἀκαίρῳ στενοχωρίᾳ. ΚΕΦ. Γʹ. Ἀλλ' ἐν τούτοις μὲν τὸ δεύτερον
ἤνυσται κεφά λαιον· τοῦ τρίτου δὲ προθεωρίαν ποιούμενοι, φαμὲν, 17.68 ὡς ἀλγεῖ
μὲν ὁ δίκαιος, καὶ οὐκ ἄν τις ἀρνήσαιτο οὐ γὰρ τῶν ἀναισθήτων ἡ ἀρετὴ, ἀλλὰ τῶν
ἐν τοῖς πάθεσι φιλοσοφούντων. Οὐ δύναται δὲ, κατὰ μὲν τὸ φαινόμενον, ὑπὸ τῆς ἐν
σαρκὶ πληγῆς δριμυ τάτως κεντούμενος· κατὰ δὲ τὸ νοούμενον, οἷα δί καιος καὶ
φιλόθεος ἀνὴρ ὁρῶν τινας σκανδαλιζομέ νους ἐπὶ τοῖς αὐτῶν παθήμασιν, ὡς τῆς τοῦ
Θεοῦ δόξης ἐπ' αὐτῷ διασυρομένης, εἰ ὁ δίκαιος ταῦτα ὑπομένει. Καὶ γὰρ ὅτε λέγει·
Ἵνα τί ἔθου με κατ' ἐντευκτήν σου; οὐκ αὐτὸς κατὰ τοῦ Θεοῦ ἐτύγχανε, μὴ γένοιτο!
τίνι γὰρ εἶχεν ἐντυγχάνειν; Ἀλλὰ τοῦτό ἐστιν ὅ φησιν· Ἵνα τί δι' ἐμὲ, ∆έσποτα, τὸ
ὄνομά σου βλασφημεῖται; Θορυβεῖται δὲ οὐδὲν ἧττον καὶ ἰλιγγιᾷ, μήπως πλείως
ἐγκατάλειψιν ὑπέστη παρὰ Θεοῦ. Οὐδὲ γὰρ οὕτω τιμωρεῖται ψυχὴ φιλόθεος, ὡς τὸ
ὑποπτεύειν καταλελεῖφθαι παρὰ Θεοῦ· καὶ μυριάκις αἱρεῖται τὸν θάνατον, ἢ μετὰ
ἀλγηδόνων καὶ τοιαύτης ὑποψίας τοῖς ζῶσιν ἐγκατα λέγεσθαι. Ἐπὶ μὲν οὖν τῇ τῶν
κτημάτων ἀπωλείᾳ καὶ τῇ τῶν παίδων ἀθρόᾳ τελευτῇ οἵας ἀφῆκε χα ριστηρίους
φωνὰς ἠκούσαμεν, καὶ ὅπως τὴν γυναῖκα ἐξεπαίδευσεν ἀπρεπές τι περὶ τοῦ
∆εσπότου λογισα μένην, καὶ ποῖα μετὰ πεῖραν καὶ ἐξουδένωσιν καὶ τὸ δριμὺ πάθος
ἐφθέγξατο, καὶ ὡς οὐδὲν αὐτὸν τῶν ἀν θρωπίνων συμπτωμάτων διεθορύβησεν· ὡς
δὲ οἱ φί λοι παρεγένοντο ἄνδρες δίκαιοι καὶ συμπαθεῖς, εὔ καιρον ᾠήθη, θεωρῶν
αὐτῶν τὴν ὑπομονὴν καὶ τὴν ἀγάπην ἐπ' αὐτῶν, εἰπεῖν καὶ δημοσιεῦσαι τὰς κατὰ
ψυχὴν ἀλγηδόνας, καὶ φθέγγεται μὲν καθ' ἱστο ρίαν ἀκίνδυνον. Ἓν γὰρ ἦν τοῦ
διαβόλου τὸ σπού δασμα, τὸ παρασκευάσαι τὸν δίκαιον βλασφημῆσαι Θεόν. Ὁ δὲ
οὐδαμῶς φαίνεται τοῦτο διαπραξάμενος, ἀλλὰ καὶ μᾶλλον εὐφημήσας, καὶ

pass_a_gloss: ...unexpectedness of the calamity also seemed unbelievable, if Job is sitting even on a dung heap and without help. And they waited to make the report sure through more persons, or also to send out and see whether the things said were true. In these things then the time was being worn away. And besides these, when they knew the truth, being kings and about to go abroad, they had the necessity first to dispose well the things of the house, and to set over the ruled those in place of themselves. All these things kept them occupied, and they were delayed. And if they had not been some very beloved and righteous men, they would not, leaving their own countries and kingdoms, have arrived for the visit, but would have fulfilled the need through others. And it is possible to consider that the postponement of the arrival was also a certain divine dispensation. For since together with the dialogue of the friends the whole of the contest was also loosed, God having given an oracle, and having recovered and crowned the righteous man, a certain divine dispensation came about, for the friends to be slow, so that the things of the disease might be stretched out, and the righteous man having contended more greatly might be proclaimed more justly by God. Verse 11. And they came to him with one mind, to comfort and to visit him. Symmachus gave it out thus: For they arranged together, coming, to suffer with him and to console him. See also from here that another time also passed, until, having sent through to one another, they made the coming-together to the same place and the arrival. Verse 12. And having sprinkled earth upon their heads. Verse 13. They sat beside him seven days and seven nights. But Scripture did not say that they were sitting beside seven days from early morning until evening, nor seven nights from evening until early morning. It is plain then that, sitting beside the greater part of the day, they withdrew to fulfil the necessary needs; and again coming back, they sat beside until much of the night, and again going away, they again came early to him. Which is indeed proper of the most genuine and most sympathetic friends. But Scripture using the common custom said thus absolutely: They sat beside him seven days and seven nights. Since also when it says that Jacob served fourteen years, and was burned together by the burning heat of the day and the frost of the night, did he then never go in under a roof? did he then meet no rest in the whole time? To speak subtly about these things is foolish talk. For, as I said, Scripture uses common custom. But since some, making comedy of Scripture, also from here tear it apart as false: For how, they say, would they have continued without food and without sleep for so many days? we were compelled to be carried away together with their untimely narrowness. Chapter 3. But in these things the second main heading has been completed; and making a fore-view of the third, we say that the righteous man feels pain, and no one would deny it; for virtue is not of the insensible, but of those philosophizing in sufferings. He is not able (read: he is in anguish), according to what appears, being stung most sharply by the blow in the flesh; but according to what is understood, as a righteous and God-loving man, seeing some being scandalized at their (the) sufferings, as the glory of God being torn apart in his case, if the righteous man endures these things. For indeed when he says: Why did you set me as a pleader against you? he himself was not pleading against God, may it not be! for to whom did he have to plead? But this is what he says: Why because of me, Master, is your name blasphemed? And he is troubled no less and is dizzy, lest perhaps he underwent fuller abandonment from God. For a God-loving soul is not so punished as by suspecting to have been left by God; and ten thousand times it chooses death, rather than with pains and such suspicion to be left among the living. Upon the loss of the possessions, then, and the sudden end of the children, what thankful voices he sent forth we heard, and how he schooled the wife who reckoned something unfitting about the Master, and what sort of things he uttered after trial and being set at nought and the sharp suffering, and how none of the human mishaps troubled him through. But when the friends arrived, righteous and sympathetic men, he thought it opportune, beholding their endurance and the love in them, to speak and to make public the pains in the soul, and he utters according to the history something without danger. For one was the zeal of the devil, to prepare the righteous man to blaspheme God. pass_b_english: … strangeness of the calamity seemed beyond belief too: that Job was really sitting on a dung heap with no one to help him. And they waited to confirm the report through more people, or else to send someone and see whether what was being said was true. In these things, then, the time was spent. Besides this, once they learned the truth, being kings and about to travel abroad, they had first to set the affairs of their houses in good order and to put others in their own place over their subjects. All this kept them busy, and they were delayed. And unless they had been men very much beloved and righteous, they would not have left their own countries and kingdoms and come to visit; they would have met the need through others.

One may also consider that the putting off of their arrival was a kind of divine dispensation. For since the whole contest was brought to its end together with the friends' dialogue, when God gave his answer and restored and crowned the righteous man, a divine dispensation came about: the friends were delayed so that the disease might be drawn out, and the righteous man, having contended the more, might be proclaimed by God the more justly.

“And they came to him with one accord, to comfort him and to visit him” (Job 2:11). Symmachus rendered it this way: “For they agreed together to come to share his suffering and to console him.” See from this too that still more time passed, until, sending messages to one another, they arranged their meeting in one place and their arrival. “And they sprinkled earth on their heads” (Job 2:12). “They sat beside him seven days and seven nights” (Job 2:13).

Scripture did not say that they sat beside him seven days from morning to evening, nor seven nights from evening to morning. It is plain, then, that they sat with him most of the day and withdrew to see to their necessary needs; then they came back again and sat with him far into the night, and going away once more, they came to him again at dawn. That is the mark of the truest and most sympathetic friends. But Scripture, following common usage, said it in this way without qualification: “They sat beside him seven days and seven nights.” For when it says too that Jacob served fourteen years and was burned by the heat of the day and the frost of the night (Genesis 31:40-41), did he then never go under a roof? Did he get no rest at all in the whole of that time? To split hairs over these things is mere chatter; for, as I said, Scripture uses common usage. But since some mock Scripture and tear it apart as false on this ground too (“How,” they say, “could they have gone on without food and without sleep for so many days?”), we have been forced to be dragged into their untimely pettiness.

But with these things the second main part has been completed. Making a preliminary survey of the third, we say that the righteous man does feel pain, and no one would deny it; for virtue does not belong to those who feel nothing, but to those who live wisely in the midst of their sufferings. [He is in anguish]: outwardly, he is stung most sharply by the blow in his flesh; inwardly, as a righteous and God-loving man, he sees some people scandalized at the sufferings, as though the glory of God were being torn apart in his case if the righteous man endures these things. For when he says, “Why have you set me up as one who pleads against you?” (Job 7:20), he himself was not pleading against God, far from it! For to whom could he make his plea? But this is what he means: “Why, Master, is your name blasphemed because of me?” And he is no less troubled and dizzy with fear that he may have suffered a fuller abandonment by God. For nothing punishes a God-loving soul so much as suspecting that it has been forsaken by God; it would choose death ten thousand times rather than be left among the living with pains and such a suspicion.

At the loss of his possessions and the sudden death of his children we have heard what words of thanksgiving he uttered, and how he corrected his wife when she had thought something unfitting about the Master, and what he said after the trial, the contempt and the sharp suffering, and how none of the mishaps that befall human beings threw him into confusion. But when the friends arrived, righteous and sympathetic men, he thought it the right moment, seeing their patience and their love, to speak and to make public the pains of his soul; and in the literal sense what he says carries no danger. For the devil had a single aim: to bring the righteous man to blaspheme God. But he clearly never did this; rather he spoke well of God and sent up words of thanksgiving.
